Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that Harmeet Dhillon resigned from leading the Justice Department's Civil Rights division.
body: Democrats flip four more House seats, strengthening new majority in lower chamber

Democrats have picked-up four more House seats, adding to their new majority. As things stand, the party has 247 seats in the lower chamber, with 35 races left to be called. Here are some of the Democrats’ latest pick-ups.

Montana’s first congressional district: Here Democrat Sam Forstag, a 32-year-old smoke jumper, beat Republican Aaron Flint, a conservative radio host. The seat is currently held by the two-term GOP representative Ryan Zinke.

Arizona’s first congressional district:Amish Shah, a Democrat and emergency room doctor, won a district held by Republican David Schweikert, who launched an unsuccessful bid for Arizona governor. Shah won the seat, which includes parts of Phoenix and Scottsdale, against GOP nominee Jay Freely, a former NFL player.

North Carolina’s sixth congressional district: Democratic state representative Cyril Jefferson beat Republican incumbent Addison McDowell – who won the seat by nearly 40 points in 2024, after it was successfully gerrymandered to benefit the GOP.

North Carolina’s 13th congressional district: Here, Democrat Paul Barringer, an attorney, defeated the first-term Republican incumbent Brad Knott. The district was also redrawn ahead of the 2024 to boost Republicans, after Democrats flipped the seat in 2022.
Democrat Richard Ojeda flips North Carolina House seat
Democrat Richard Ojeda has flipped North Carolina’s ninth congressional district, beating two-term Republican incumbent Richard Hudson in a seat that has been solidly red for the last 14 years.
Nithya Raman elected mayor of Los Angeles, defeating incumbent Karen Bass

Nithya Raman was elected to serve as the mayor of Los Angeles, eking out a narrow win over incumbent Karen Bass, in a major shake-up in local politics that reflects the growing dissatisfaction with the direction of the city.

The progressive urban planner had served on LA’s city council since 2020. She caused a stir when she entered the race earlier this year hours before the filing deadline – and shortly after endorsing Bass for re-election – and her campaign was once viewed as a long shot.

In the months leading up to the midterm elections, Donald Trump’s administration waged an aggressive effort to sow doubt about the results, intimidate voters and election officials, and signal they would use the power of the federal government to challenge the electoral process.

But when the results came in on Tuesday night, revealing a huge blowout for the GOP, Trump did something almost unprecedented: he accepted the results. Trump said he was “absolutely willing” to accept the outcome and looked forward to working with Democrats. With the exception of the 2024 election, which he won and Republicans performed well in, Trump has raised doubt about every presidential race and midterm since his first election in 2016.

Perhaps he had no choice. “It was essentially too big to rig,” an unnamed Trump adviser told CNN. But even before the results were known, many of Trump’s election interference attempts simply never materialized.

Administration officials had declined to rule out the possibility of deploying immigration agents to the polls. There were worries that the 1,000 justice department monitors deployed to voting sites would attempt to meaningfully disrupt the voting process. Some thought Trump would try something outlandish like trying to seize voting machines or ballots. Others speculated Republicans could try a longshot maneuver to block new members of Congress from being seated on January 3.
None of that happened, and the certification of new members in January looks like it will go smoothly.

Another House race we’re keeping an eye on at the moment is Maine’s second congressional district, a Republican stronghold that Donald Trump carried in the last presidential election, despite losing the state. As of now, 95% of the vote has been counted, with GOP nominee Paul LePage leading against Democrat Matt Dunlap.

A short while ago, Dunlap conceded in the race for the seat that moderate Jared Golden holds. LePage would now be the sole Republican in the Maine congressional delegation after Senator Susan Collins, the five-term incumbent, lost her re-election bid to Troy Jackson – a major defeat after 30 years in office.
We’ll bring you the final result as soon as its announced.

Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer told a gathering at the Democratic leaning Center for American Progress, that in spite of the Democratic party’s victories on election day, voters were still wary of the party.

“Millions of Americans voted for us because of frustration with Trump, not out of love for the Democratic Party. Many Americans across the political spectrum are still skeptical of our party and that’s OK. We are fortunate to have the opportunity to earn back their trust,” he said.
The 75-year-old lawmaker – widely seen as a centrist – warned about what he called the “false choice” in the Democratic party. “Populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said.

Schumer said messaging before the election was intentional and disciplined. He said Democratic leadership in Congress made the decision to embrace a core message while campaigning against Republicans: “Cost, chaos and corruption.”
And following up on this, Harmett Dhillon has told Fox News today that she actually resigned three weeks ago.
“And Susie [Wiles] asked me to please wait until after the midterms,” she said, referring to the White House chief of staff.
According to Fox, Dhillon said she told Wiles she believed she had “accomplished everything” she came to Washington to do and wanted to return to private practice.
Dhillon also stressed that was “not asked to resign”.

When it comes to a potential pardon from the president to shield her from congressional oversight when Democrats take control in the new year, Dhillon told Fox: “I have no idea. I haven’t ever discussed that with him, asked for it.”
She added: “And I have done nothing, in my opinion, that would require that, but, you know, that’s up to the president.”
Todd Blanche confirms Harmeet Dhillon's resignation from justice department

Attorney general Todd Blanche has now confirmed that Harmeet Dhillon, an ally of Donald Trump, has resigned from her position leading the justice department’s Civil Rights division. In a statement, Blanche said that today he accepted her notice.

“She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor. The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors,” Blanche said.
As I noted earlier, Bloomberg reported that Dhillon was planning to leave her post.
Democrats flip four more House seats, strengthening new majority in lower chamber

Democrats have picked-up four more House seats, adding to their new majority. As things stand, the party has 247 seats in the lower chamber, with 35 races left to be called. Here are some of the Democrats’ latest pick-ups.

Montana’s first congressional district: Here Democrat Sam Forstag, a 32-year-old smoke jumper, beat Republican Aaron Flint, a conservative radio host. The seat is currently held by the two-term GOP representative Ryan Zinke.

Arizona’s first congressional district:Amish Shah, a Democrat and emergency room doctor, won a district held by Republican David Schweikert, who launched an unsuccessful bid for Arizona governor. Shah won the seat, which includes parts of Phoenix and Scottsdale, against GOP nominee Jay Freely, a former NFL player.

North Carolina’s sixth congressional district: Democratic state representative Cyril Jefferson beat Republican incumbent Addison McDowell – who won the seat by nearly 40 points in 2024, after it was successfully gerrymandered to benefit the GOP.

North Carolina’s 13th congressional district: Here, Democrat Paul Barringer, an attorney, defeated the first-term Republican incumbent Brad Knott. The district was also redrawn ahead of the 2024 to boost Republicans, after Democrats flipped the seat in 2022.
Top justice department lawyer plans to resign amid Republican midterms defeat - report
Harmeet Dhillon, the justice department lawyer who leads the Civil Rights division, is planning to resign, according to Bloomberg.
Citing four people familiar with the matter, Bloomberg reports that Dhillon has told allies that she would leave the DoJ after the midterm elections.
The justice department did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment on the matter.

As my colleague Sam Levine reports, Dhillon – who once worked as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer – oversees the justice department division responsible for enforcing America’s federal civil rights laws. Since arriving at the justice department in April 2025, Dhillon has dropped dozens of anti-discrimination cases seeking relief for minorities in voting, housing, policing and employment and instead reorienting the division around preventing discrimination against white Americans. Hundreds of attorneys have left the division.

Dhillon made her name in Maga circles by taking on culture-war cases as a San Francisco lawyer and became a fixture in rightwing media, appearing often on Fox shows. She has filed various lawsuits over election “integrity” issues and supported Trump’s quests to overturn results in 2020.
Washington state passes ballot measure banning trans girls from school sports
Sam Levin
Voters in Washington state have passed a ballot measure banning transgender girls from playing on girls’ sports teams, a major loss for LGBTQ+ rights in a solidly Democratic state.

The measure says students in elementary, middle and high school who want to join girls’ athletics must first submit statements from their healthcare providers verifying their “biological sex”. Opponents have raised alarms the measure may force girls to endure “invasive and extreme” genital exams to participate in school sports.
Initiative 638 passed with support from nearly 57% of voters as of Thursday morning, though votes were still being counted.

More than 25 states across the US have adopted similar bans on trans youth athletes, mostly through legislation pushed by Republican lawmakers. Voters in Arizona and Nebraska approved similar ballot measures this week, and a ban proposed in Colorado was leading in early results, but that race has not yet been called.
Abdul El-Sayed says pick for Senate majority leader is about 'action' after refusing to back Schumer on campaign trail
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senator-elect in Michigan, said that the new majority in the upper chamber needs “action” from their leader, in an interview in CNN.

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed refused to back Senator Chuck Schumer, who currently serves as the minority leader. Schumer initially backed El-Sayed’s opponent, Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, before supporting El-Sayed in the general election and blasting Stevens for her “despicable betrayal” in endorsing Republican Mike Rogers.
Speaking to CNN, El-Sayed reiterated that Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat, would be an “amazing Senate majority leader”, but didn’t completely rule out supporting Schumer.

“It seems like [Van Hollen] is quite interested in another goal politically, which, you know, would mean that would be very difficult for him to do that,” El-Sayed said, referring to reports about the Senator’s presidential ambitions. “A vote is a choice between two or more options. I don’t know what those options are. But here’s what I’ll say. We need action.”
He added:

I don’t know who’s stepping up and saying, I want to be Senate majority leader … if we have another option, I’m going to look at that and say, who is best placed to get us action, to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All.
Was Elon Musk the US midterms’ biggest loser? – podcast

The tech industry spent big on the midterms, but it turned out to be a poor investment. Elon Musk poured a staggering $446m dollars into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, but his efforts didn’t pay off. Democrats won every one of the five Senate races where Musk’s America Pac spent the most money backing Republican candidates.

In today’s episode our Stateside podcast Carter Sherman and Kai Wright are joined by the Guardian’s US tech editor, Blake Montgomery, to ask what the “blue tsunami” will mean for Musk and the wider tech industry. Will this spell the end of AI datacenters? And if so, what could this mean for the US economy?

There are “knives out” at the Pentagon as Trump administration officials reel from the thrashing dealt to the GOP in this week’s midterms – and Trump is looking for someone to blame after his unpopular war on Iran sealed the party’s fate, according to the Washington Post (paywall) this morning.

According to the Post’s sources, rather than place blame with his defense secretary Pete Hegseth, Trump could be more likely to instead sack General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Admiral Brad Cooper, who has overseen the war.

Hegseth has survived many a controversy in his short tenure, a number of which – from Signal-gate to alleged potential war crimes – many thought should’ve been career-ending. But he has held Trump’s confidence time and time again, including after reports that he misled the president over the course of the war.
I’m at the US Capitol, where there’s not a lot going on, since lawmakers are not scheduled to reconvene until next week.
But the good vibes Democrats are feeling after their dramatic victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections are real, particularly in deep-blue Washington DC.
A shirtless man just jogged by, pointing at the Capitol and yelling, “we got it back!” A group of what looked like visiting students cheered with him.
Cruz says midterms were ‘Watergate-level repudiation’ for Republicans

Joining the chorus of Republicans – who have blasted their party’s poor performance in the midterms – is sitting senator Ted Cruz, of Texas, who said the GOP were handed an “ass-kicking” this cycle, losing control of Congress.
“It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” he said on an episode of his podcast, ‘The Verdict’.

He noted, like vice-president JD Vance, that there wasn’t a turnout issue. “Instead, our voters Republicans, Libertarians, Independents, showed up and voted and rejected our candidates, voting Democrat,” Cruz said, noting that economic anxiety appeared to be top of mind this cycle.
“Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high,” he added. “Too many Republican politicians seem like they didn’t understand or they didn’t care.”
Cruz, who is up for re-election in 2030 is also a contender as a Republican candidate for president.

“We need to listen and respond. We need to champion economic policies that make a real difference in working people’s lives, and we need to deal with the consequences,” Cruz added, noting that he called Democratic senator-elect James Talarico to congratulate him on his victory.

articles.headline: Oil prices rebound slightly as Iran claims new attacks on ships
keyFacts: International oil prices rose 2.2% to $96.70 per barrel on Thursday, recovering part of a nearly 9% drop following the U.S. midterm elections.
Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow to discuss strengthening bilateral ties and building a gas pipeline from Russia to Iran.
Oman announced it is continuing talks with Iran to create a joint control system for the Strait of Hormuz to end the state of war and secure maritime traffic.
body: What to know about the Iran war:

- Oil prices fell sharply after the midterm elections, as markets appeared to hope the results might push President Trump toward a deal to end and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Commercial ships in the region continue coming under attack, however, and hitting sea mines, according to Iranian authorities.

- As a senior Iranian security official met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin amid uncertainty over President Trump's next move, Moscow warned Russian citizens not to visit Iran, citing the "risk of a new escalation."

- Oman said Thursday that it was still in talks with Iran aimed at creating a system for the nations to jointly control traffic through the vital shipping lanes of the strait, which the Omani foreign ministry said could "end the state of war and prevent renewed confrontations in the region."
Putin, Iran's security chief discuss building oil pipeline from Russia to Iran

Russian President Vladimir Putin received Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between their two countries, including a pipeline to import Russian gas.

Speaking to journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighbouring countries."
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Iranian foreign minister talks to counterparts from several Middle East countries

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spent much of the day on calls with his counterparts from several Middle Eastern countries, including Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey.

In total, Araghchi held calls with nine different countries in the Middle East. Few details were shared about what was discussed on the calls, simply nodding to "diplomatic efforts to maintain stability in the region."

Notably, Pakistan was one of those countries involved as they have been very closely involved as mediators in U.S.-Iran peace talks. Araghchi spoke to their foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, on Thursday evening.

Araghchi also spoke to Saudi foreign ministers Faisal bin Farhan and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, despite accusations of Iranian involvement in attacks on that country by the Houthi militia in Yemen.
Trump administration held talks with Iran on deporting Iranians during the war, AP reports
President Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

The documents show the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."

"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.

"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."
"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal."
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Houthi drone disrupts traffic at Saudi airport, group says
The Houthis took credit for disrupting travel using a drone at King Fahd International Airport on Thursday.
"We targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam using a drone and our operation caused a disruption of air navigation at the airport," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.

The city of Dammam, which is located in the oil-rich eastern part of Saudi Arabia, and King Fahd airport have been regular targets for Houthi attacks. Multiple drones have disrupted traffic at the airport this week, according to past announcements.
Two people were killed in a Houthi strike on King Fahd airport on Oct. 22.
3rd U.S. aircraft carrier strike group heading for Mideast to make stop in Singapore, delaying arrival

The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its associated strike group will make a port call in Singapore Friday and will not reach the Middle East for at least another two weeks, a U.S. official told CBS News on Thursday.
There are already two carrier strike groups in the region and, which officials say is sufficient firepower to execute any commands issued by President Trump.

Mr. Trump has not signaled yet, in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, whether he intends to order major new strikes on Iran — an option he kept on the table with repeated statements ahead of Tuesday's voting.
Oil prices rebound slightly after huge drop in wake of U.S. midterm elections
The initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit Thursday.
The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, considered the international standard, rose 2.2% to $96.70, recovering a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before.
Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
CBS/AP
As top Iranian official meets Putin, Russia warns citizens not to visit Iran, citing "risk of a new escalation"

Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, met Thursday in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin to deliver a message from Iran's supreme leader, according to the Iranian government.

They met amid uncertainty over President Trump's next move on Iran in the wake of U.S. midterm election results that represented a major rebuke of his policies, including, he has admitted, the decision to launch the war with Iran alongside Israel more than eight months ago.

Mr. Trump said repeatedly ahead of the Tuesday vote that he had yet to make a decision on whether to order major new attacks on Iran or to agree a deal to end the war, which Tehran has so far refused to do until the U.S. accepts its core demands to end its naval blockade, ensure a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, and ease sanctions.
During the Rezaei-Putin meeting in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned Russian citizens against all travel to Iran.

"Given the continued risk of a new escalation around Iran, our recommendations to Russian citizens remain unchanged," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters in Moscow. "We recommend temporarily refraining from traveling to that country until the situation is resolved. We also ask our compatriots already in Iran to exercise vigilance and avoid crowds, public events, and areas near military and government facilities."
She said the guidance was "based on the official information disseminated by Tehran," without providing any further detail.
Iran again claims it has no role in backing the Houthis in Yemen's civil war

The Iranian Foreign Ministry renewed the regime's rejection on Thursday of longtime and widely held beliefs that Tehran materially supports the Houthi rebels fighting the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen's decade-long civil war. The conflict intensified a couple months ago and quickly became the most active and deadly front in the intertwined conflicts in the Middle East.

Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the latest accusation of Iranian support for the Houthis, made Monday by European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, "baseless," and said Iran "strongly denied claims that Iranian military experts were present in Yemen."

The U.S. government, along with many other Western nations and the NATO alliance, have demanded for years that Iran stop supporting the Houthis. The support, according to these nations, includes financial backing, weapons and other equipment, and direct coordination and training.

In July, not long before the Yemen war escalated and the Houthis started launching attacks on Saudi airports in response, the Reuters news agency reported that Iran had flown commanders from its powerful, heavily sanctioned Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, along with equipment related to missiles and drones, to Yemen bolster the Houthis' ability to threaten global energy supplies in the Red Sea.
Since then, have killed at least 20 people.

In her remarks Monday, the EU's Kallas said "all Houthi military action must end immediately. We call on all actors, including Iran to cease all military support to the Houthis, in violation of several United Nations Security Council resolutions."
Iran has always denied supporting the Houthis.
Oman says still working with Iran on joint control system for Strait of Hormuz "that would end the state of war"

Oman's government said Thursday that, in a phone call between the Omani and Iranian foreign ministers, both men "stressed the importance of moving from the stage of de-escalating tensions to one of establishing sustainable understandings based on practical arrangements to ensure the safety of maritime routes and joint technical mechanisms to secure the smooth flow of international trade and energy, in a manner that would end the state of war and prevent renewed confrontations in the region."

Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamoud Al Busaidi and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi "reviewed the latest developments in communications and discussions aimed at reaching practical, political, and technical understandings that would enable the resumption of unimpeded maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz," the Omani Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Iran and Oman have discussed for months implementing a joint mechanism to control commercial traffic through the strait, over which both Iran and the U.S. insist they currently have dominion. Iran started threatening and attacking ships in the region in response to the U.S. and Israel jointly launching the ongoing war against the Islamic Republic at the end of February, and those attacks continue despite U.S. assertions that the strait is now open safe to use.

According to Oman, the ministers emphasized in their Thursday call that any future "understandings must be based on respect for the sovereignty of states, consideration of the legitimate interests of all parties, and the creation of appropriate conditions for restoring dialogue and negotiation processes and addressing the outstanding issues underlying the escalation."
Another oil tanker hits mine, catches fire near Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
An oil tanker hit a mine, caught fire and was immobilized east of the Strait of Hormuz early on Thursday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corp navy said, according to IRNA, Tehran's official news agency.
The navy said the tanker had switched off its identification and navigation systems, a tactic used by vessels seeking to avoid detection by Iran.
The IRGC has declared the strait "unsafe and closed" to vessels trying to go through the vital waterway without coordination with Tehran.
Saudi coalition says it intercepted Houthi missile fired at Medina region

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Thursday that a ballistic missile fired by the group at the Medina region — home to one of Islam's holiest cities — had been intercepted.
"Air defense intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Medina region," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post.
Tanker hit by 2 projectiles north of Qatar, British military says
A tanker was hit by two unidentified projectiles in the Persian Gulf about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, Qatar, a British military tracking agency said Thursday.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre (KKMTO) said the status of the crew, damage assessment and environmental impact weren't known.
Iran says two tankers and tugboat caught fire in Strait of Hormuz
Two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said, local media reported on Thursday.
Since the outbreak of the Iran war on Feb. 28, Tehran has severely restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.

In response, the United States has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel through the strait. The U.S. Central Command said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via the strait since summer.

"Last night, in two separate incidents, a large oil tanker attempting to pass through the illegal passageway south of the Strait of Hormuz suffered a fire after striking a mine and was brought to a halt," the Guard told Iran's Fars news agency.
"Another supertanker was halted by a massive fire while exiting the eastern Strait of Hormuz. A tugboat that had approached the supertanker to extinguish the fire also caught fire."
Fars also reported the IRGC navy's electronic warfare unit had taken control of two LUCAS drones, a U.S.-developed model short for Low-cost Uncrewed Combat Attack System.
Reelected Colorado Rep. Jason Crow on Iran after midterms: "The war has got to end"

Colorado Democratic Rep. Jason Crow, who has won his midterm reelection bid, told CBS News how Democrats will address the war with Iran as the party takes control of Congress next year, saying, "The war has got to end."

"Americans never wanted it to begin with. Americans for years have wanted to end this constant cycle of conflict in the Middle East. In fact, Donald Trump even campaigned on that," Crow, a member of the House Armed Services Committee, told Major Garrett on "The Takeout" on Wednesday night.
Asked whether Congress plans to address the war through war power resolutions or
using the power of appropriations to take away funding, Crow replied: "Yes."

"We have voted on seven resolutions and passed two of them so far. We should continue to take votes. Let people stand up," he added. "Appropriations is one of our most powerful tools. We have to be willing to do that too."
When it comes to the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Crow said that future "should be short."
"Pete Hegseth is incompetent. He was never qualified to do this, never should have been in the position to begin with. He needs to go," he said.
U.S. sanctions Indian companies over alleged maritime fraud aiding Iran

The United States on Wednesday issued sanctions targeting what it described as a "vast criminal network" run by two Indian nationals that was aiding Iran's shadow fleet of oil tankers in committing maritime fraud.
In a statement, the U.S. Treasury said the network aided Iranian vessels in sailing under false flags and in gaining fake maritime certifications.

The move was the latest in a tightening web of U.S. sanctions targeting Iran since August, when Washington announced it would be seeking the "economic asphyxiation" of the country in conjunction with its military campaign.

"As we have said many times, under Operation Economic Outcast, you are either with us or against us," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has in the past threatened sanctions against any country or company that aids Iran, regardless of its relationship with Washington.
Wednesday's sanctions named Indian nationals Suniel Kumar Sharma and his wife Jaspreet Preeti Shahid as operating a large-scale maritime fraud network from their base in Chandigarh.

"Purporting to represent nations from nearly every continent, from Guyana to Eswatini and Laos, Sharma and Shahid have allowed the Iranian shadow fleet ... to evade international restrictions on their operation," the Treasury said in a statement.
Head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council takes shot at U.S. in wake of election
The powerful head of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council gave credit to his country for the rebuke of President Trump in the midterm elections.

"The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz — and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington," Mohsen Rezaei said on X. "Meanwhile, Americans got stuck with the bill for his war."
"Anyone who takes on Iran will pay the price — from the battlefield to their own doorstep," he added.

Vice President JD Vance reportedly reached out to Rezaei last week about discussing conditions for a ceasefire and negotiations on the war. It's unclear how the midterm elections will affect Iran's negotiations to end the war, but President Trump said he did not regret the attacks.
Following Democratic wave, Schumer says war in Iran "must end"

Top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer said Wednesday that the Iran war "must end" and suggested his party's incoming majority in Congress could use their control over government funding to press for that goal.

"The American people don't know what the heck we're fighting for in Iran," Schumer told journalists. "He's never made it clear he changes his mind day to day and minute to minute. This war must end. It must end."
He later noted the "power of the purse" is "one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people."
Schumer and Democrats in Congress have been pushing to pass war powers resolutions throughout the war. The bills would force President Trump to remove soldiers from Iran.
The longtime New York Democrat also intimated funding could be pulled in order to force the war to come to an end.
Exit polls most think the U.S. made the wrong decision to take that military action, including about a quarter of Republicans.
AFP/CBS
Trump says it's "largely true" the war in Iran cost Republicans in midterms
President Trump said it's "probably true" the war in Iran was responsible in the midterm elections, specifically the cost of gas related to the war.

"Well, I think it's largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term," he told reporters at an event related to the ballroom's construction. "But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I'd have to do it again. Because long term, it's the only answer. You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."
Mr. Trump was responding to a question about Vice President JD Vance on the war in a post on X earlier in the day.

"But I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different," Trump continued. "We've totally broken their military. The navy's gone. Their air force is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone."
Red Cross delivers first supplies to Yemen's Taiz in over a month
The International Committee of the Red Cross said it delivered medical supplies into Taiz on Wednesday for the first time in weeks since the Iran-backed Houthis surrounded the Yemeni city.

The ICRC "delivered four trucks of essential medical supplies to Taiz city, including surgical kits to help hospitals treat weapon-wounded patients," it said in a statement. "This is the ICRC's first delivery of medical supplies to hospitals in Taiz City since 23 September, just before the intensification of fighting in the area."

Taiz, which is located in western Yemen, has become the focal point of the war between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni army. In late summer, the Houthis swept through the western part of the country and acquired wide swaths of land up to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which forms the southern opening to the Red Sea.
Taiz, the country's third-largest city, was left isolated from international aid groups when the Houthis rapidly took over the territory.
AFP/CBS
Brent crude drops under $100, lowest level since September
Brent crude oil, the international standard, dropped significantly on Wednesday, falling under $100 a barrel for the first time since September.
The price was down over 8% at noon Eastern time, falling to about $94 a barrel. The cost hasn't been under $95 a barrel since Sept. 1.
Brent crude last closed at under $100 a barrel on Sept. 30. The cost then consistently rose to a high of $116 per barrel on Oct. 23. It has dropped since, closing at $103 per barrel on Tuesday.

The decrease comes a day after Democrats won by a landslide in midterm elections, rebuking President Trump and his position on the war with Iran. Democrats, who have already voted several times in the House to restore war powers to Congress, are likely to pursue de-escalation in the conflict.
Trump asking advisers if Pete Hegseth should go, sources say

President Trump has been asking advisers around him and on the phone whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should stay in his job, following Republicans' catastrophic losses Tuesday night, multiple sources familiar with the matter tell CBS News.

Some White House aides have predicted some of the blame for GOP midterm losses will be trained on Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine, who both played big roles in guidance on the Iran war.

Still, other sources said the president hasn't decided to replace Hegseth. Before the election, Democrats were already trying to impeach Hegseth, and the likelihood of an impeachment effort could increase with Democrats holding strong majorities in both chambers.
Vance blames Iran conflict for GOP midterm defeats: "The reason we lost is the war"
In his first public comments on the election results, Vice President JD Vance said the reason Republicans were handedly defeated in the House and Senate is because of the war in Iran.

"The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," Vance wrote in a post on X. "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest. But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

The vice president, a possible 2028 contender, said many voters who backed the Trump-Vance ticket in 2024 cast their ballots for Democrats in 2026 for four reasons: to end the war with Iran, focus on the cost of living and inflation, put America first and change the U.S. relationship with Israel.
"Our voters showed up," Vance wrote. "And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats."
Iran claims to have shot down another U.S. MQ-1 drone over island in Strait of Hormuz

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement Wednesday it had shot down a U.S. MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, claiming it was the 15th of the type downed by Iranian forces during the war.
In September, U.S. officials told CBS News on condition of anonymity that Iranian forces had, at that time, brought down at least two MQ-1s.

The U.S. military has fielded two principal MQ-1 variants: the Predator, which became a fixture of U.S. operations in Iraq and Afghanistan before the Air Force retired it in 2018, and the Gray Eagle, a larger Predator-derived aircraft still operated by the Army, including its special operations forces.

Both the Predator and Gray Eagle were designed for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions but they can also carry Hellfire missiles for striking targets. In the Strait of Hormuz, these unmanned aircraft can provide U.S. forces with persistent surveillance over the narrow waterway while also tracking Iranian military activity and monitoring threats to both American forces and commercial shipping.
The Air Force's older MQ-1 Predators have largely been retired, but if Iran has in fact shot down 10 of the aircraft, the loss would still equate to roughly $40 million.
Houthis claim to have struck Saudi Arabian capital's King Khalid airport again with ballistic missile
Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen claimed Wednesday to have struck King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi Arabian capital Riyadh with a ballistic missile, causing "extensive damage."

Saudi Arabia, despite its significant size, wealth and military advantage over the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels, by the group. Previous Houthi strikes on Saudi airports in October killed at least 20 people, most of them at King Khalid.

In a statement shared Wednesday on social media, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that the the Riyadh airport was "unsafe" and he renewed the group's "call to all international airlines, employees, and travelers not to travel through Saudi airspace, as it is unsafe, with the exception of the airspace over the holy areas of Mecca and Medina."
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the Houthi claim to have hit the airport again on Wednesday.
Houthis claim series of successful attacks on Saudi Arabian forces
The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claimed Wednesday to have shot down a Chinese-made armed reconnaissance drone operated by Saudi Arabia over Yemen's southern Taiz province.

In a statement shared online by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said it was the 10th Saudi operated drone of the type downed by the rebels during the current escalation of Yemen's civil war, in which Saudi Arabia backs the Yemeni government.

Saree said in a string of social media posts that the Houthis had also "carried out an operation targeting Saudi enemy forces" with six ballistic missiles east of Yemen's al-Jawf province, "leaving dozens dead and wounded and destroying a number of military vehicles."
Other Houthi operations targeted a radar installation north of Jizan, Saudi Arabia, and a Saudi military encampment in Najran, he said.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the Houthi claims.
Iranians take to streets of Tehran for pro-regime rally

People marched through central Tehran Wednesday in a major pro-regime rally to mark the 47th anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. embassy in the Iranian capital, chanting anti-U.S. and Israel slogans.
Some held signs calling for revenge for the killing of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei at the outset of the ongoing war, while others mocked President Trump.
"We are not happy about the surge in oil prices," said one woman, who gave AFP only her last name, Mahmoudkhani.
"But there is some satisfaction in knowing we are no longer living this torment alone. We, alone, have been suffering under sanctions for so many years," she added.
Some echoed Iranian officials doubts' that the election results would change much for Iranians.

"Whether it is the Democrats or the Republicans, there is no difference for us," Mohammad, a 42-year-old civil servant, told AFP. "The US government's approach toward the Iranian people has unfortunately remained the same over the past 50 years."
CBS/AFP
Statement attributed to Iran's supreme leader plays down hopes of shift in U.S. war policy

A statement attributed to Iran's elusive Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Wednesday said anyone expecting a shift in U.S. policy regarding the war with Iran in the wake of the American midterm elections was "seriously mistaken."

"Those who still harbor even the slightest hope that the behavior of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken," said the statement published on Khamenei's website.

Khamenei was named as the successor to his father, former leader Ali Khamenei, soon after the older man was killed in the initial wave of U.S.-Israeli strikes at the outset of the war. U.S. officials believe the younger Khamenei was seriously wounded in the same strike, and he has not been seen or heard from directly at all since being named the new supreme leader.

President Trump has said the war with Iran was partly responsible for the dismal midterm election results for his Republican party this week, but that he does not regret his decision to launch it in conjunction with Israel.
In the message released Wednesday, Khamenei warned that "should such aggressions be repeated, the war's scope will become much wider."
CBS/AFP
Trump says U.S. has no immediate plan to strike Iran, despite being "locked and loaded"

President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran, after keeping the option on the table for weeks ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

"We seem to be getting everything we want," the FT quoted Mr. Trump as saying, referring to the current stalemate with Iran. While major fighting stopped weeks ago, the standoff has seen the Islamic Republic continue threatening and attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, which in turn has kept global oil prices 60% to 70% higher than they were before the war started, driving up consumer costs across the globe.
Asked whether there would be a new attack on Iran later this week, Mr. Trump said "we're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it."

Despite the impasse, the president claimed the current circumstances were "brilliant," with oil still reaching global markets from the Persian Gulf, including under U.S. military escort through the Strait of Hormuz.
"If you think about it, we haven't really had a war with them in a long time. Six months, maybe more," asserted Mr. Trump.
China says avoiding more conflict in Middle East a "top priority"
China's foreign ministry said Wednesday that avoiding a resumption of the conflict between Iran and the U.S. was a "top priority" in its diplomatic efforts in the region.

"The top priority is to avoid the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East that would bring disaster to the region's people," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing.

China will "support Iran and the U.S. in resolving disputes through negotiations, promote finding a political settlement to the Yemen issue, to help reach a proper and comprehensive solution for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz," she added.
China is an economic ally of Iran. Chinese purchases of Iranian crude oil amount to nearly 45% of the Iranian government's budget, according to a U.S. government report from March 2025.
Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia for visits "aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions," the foreign ministry said Wednesday.
CBS/AFP
Lebanese prime minister warns of "risks of renewed war," and of Lebanon being dragged in again

In a message seemingly directed at the Iran-backed group Hezbollah, Lebanon's prime minister warned Wednesday against any moves that could pull the country into renewed fighting between Iran and the U.S. and Israel.

"Faced with the risks of renewed war in the region, I renew my warning of the dangers of dragging Lebanon into a new senseless adventure in service of outside interests," Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday, without explicitly mentioning Hezbollah.

Southern Lebanon has been a major front in the interlinked regional conflicts, with fighting between Iran's Hezbollah allies and Israel's military driving tens of thousands of people from their homes and killing almost 9,000 since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Hezbollah, long a powerful political and paramilitary force in the country, pulled Lebanon directly into the war with Israel by launching strikes on the Jewish state in support of Hamas after the 2023 terror attacks sparked the war in Gaza, and then by firing rockets and missiles in support of Iran after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes commenced on Feb. 28.

The Lebanon conflict has proven to be a major sticking point in negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, as Tehran has consistently rejected any peace deal with Washington that does not also end fighting in Lebanon and Gaza.

A fragile ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Hezbollah in June has halted most large-scale fighting between the two sides, but Israeli forces still occupy a large section of southern Lebanon, and there are sporadic attacks by both sides.
"We do not accept the country again becoming a theater for the conflict of others," Salam added, saying Lebanon had "already paid a heavy price."

President Trump threatened repeatedly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections to renew strikes on Iran, but he told the Financial Times as the results came in Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order attacks.
CBS/AFP
Four tankers catch fire while transiting Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military says
Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said Wednesday, after it warned no one would benefit from a return to war.

"Four non-compliant oil tankers attempting to pass through the prohibited passage south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed after striking naval mines and are still burning," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement quoted by state TV.
"Two other non-compliant ships or vessels have also been halted," they said
The attacks come even as a diplomatic push is underway aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran. Indirect talks via Qatari, Pakistani and Saudi mediators are understood to be underway.

Although both sides previously expressed some hope of reaching an agreement, Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council on Tuesday cast doubt on progress toward a deal, calling the U.S. response to their demands "not convincing."
CBS/AFP
Iran says midterm results reflect rejection of war
Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday the midterm election results mean Americans have rejected the war with his country.
"Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
He cited the increased cost of living or "conscience" as two of the possible reasons for the widespread Republican losses in Tuesday's vote.
"If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added.
Trump acknowledges war with Iran partially to blame for GOP's election defeat
President Trump acknowledged on Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections.
In a phone interview with Fox News, Mr. Trump said "part of it was Iran" when explaining the result of the elections, but that "at the same time, people understand the importance of what I've done."
In a separate interview with the The Wall Street Journal, the president reiterated his comments and added that he does not regret starting the war with Tehran.
"I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," he told the newspaper.
Qatar is said to expect feedback from U.S. and Iran on latest peace proposal within 36 hours

Qatari mediators expect feedback within 36 hours from Iranian and U.S. negotiators on new ideas aimed at getting both sides closer to a deal to end the war, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing an official briefed on the talks.
"The mediators came up with a new suggestion to move the process along, and it's currently being studied by the two sides," the official told Reuters.

Efforts to reach a deal to prevent a return to fighting between Iran and the U.S. have ramped up recently. President Trump has said he is still open to an agreement, but has also threatened to resume major U.S. strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S.
On the eve of the elections, Mr. Trump again expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached, claiming Tehran wanted a settlement "as soon as possible."
Iranian officials declared Monday that the ball "is in the U.S. court" and they said Iran's core demands to end the war would not be altered.

articles.headline: Gavin Newsom lets all of California’s 548 death row inmates escape ultimate punishment
keyFacts: Governor Gavin Newsom announced on Thursday that he will commute all 548 death-row inmates in California.
Newsom stated that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California values and undermines the legal system.
The California Supreme Court must approve the commutations for inmates with multiple felony convictions.
body: Gov. Gavin Newsom dropped a bombshell move on Thursday to commute all 548 death-row inmates in California.
In a letter to Californians, Newsom said that he understood that victims are angry at the horrendousness of the inmates’ crimes.
“But as Governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them,” he wrote. “We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honor their victims.”
Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!

“I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us,” Newsom explained.
“I know we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, first among them justice and human decency.”
Newsom said the decision to mass commute was one of the “most difficult” in his career, and he said he’s deeply aware how it will trigger unpleasant memories of victims’ surviving family members.

“I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss,” the Democratic governor said. “I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action.”
In his long-winded letter, Newsom said he ruled out the idea of not commuting inmates with the “worst of the worst” crimes.

“I carefully considered different categories of capital crimes and offender characteristics. I have learned, however, from speaking with the victims harmed by these crimes, that each experiences their loss as the worst of the worst,” he said.

“I have concluded that attempting to distinguish among crimes and offenders for clemency would inadvertently create two classes of murder victims—those whose perpetrators deserve the death penalty and then the rest.”

Conversations over the mass clemency for some of the state’s most notorious criminals ramped up after Tennessee’s botched execution of Christa Pike, which went horribly wrong when two doses of the highly potent sedative pentobarbital failed to kill her, The New York Times reported.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006, even though it houses the nation’s largest death-row population. That’s partially because Newsom introduced the state’s moratorium on executions through an executive order in 2019.

Despite the moratorium, prosecutors in California are still able to seek the death penalty. More than 200 people have received a death sentence in California since the last execution in 2006, CalMatters reported.
Newsom in his letter said he respected the fact that Californians actually voted in the past to keep the death penalty on the books.
“But the constitution also gave every governor clemency authority, and that power exists for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice. For me, this is that moment,” Newsom added.

Pressure was growing for the governor to enact a mass death-row commutation even before the Pike incident, though the California Supreme Court would have to approve commutations for people with multiple felony convictions.
A mass commutation in California could slash the total number of condemned inmates across the country by more than a quarter.
Of the 548 people on death row, 529 of them are men. Around 45 of them would be immediately subject to execution without Newsom’s moratorium, according to the governor’s office.

A commutation could spare the likes of Richard Allen Davis — convicted in 1996 of kidnapping and murdering 12-year-old Polly Klaas — and serial killer Charles Ng, who was convicted of 11 first-degree murders, among other condemned criminals in the Golden State.
The governor said he will take all the backlash.

“I also acknowledge that this clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians. This will always weigh heavily on me. As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution,” he concluded.

articles.headline: Eight killed in series of shootings in western Turkey
keyFacts: Eight people were killed and one was seriously injured in a series of shootings across Afyonkarahisar province in western Turkey.
Turkish state media reported that the victims were found in multiple locations and included two teachers.
Authorities stated that the suspect fled the scene, abandoned a vehicle, and was later arrested in Eskişehir province.
body: - Published
Eight people have been killed and one seriously injured in a series of shootings in western Turkey.
The attacks took place in the Afyonkarahisar province on Thursday, with victims found in several locations in three separate vehicles, according to local reports.
The suspect fled, triggering a manhunt, and authorities later said he had been arrested in EskiÅehir province.
CCTV footage published in Turkish media showed a man in a black jacket, white trousers and glasses clutching a long weapon as he stood by a red minivan.

Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency reported that three people were killed near Ayazini village and three others near Kiyir village. In Yukaritandir, two women were found injured and later died in hospital.
Two teachers were reportedly among the dead.
Local media said roads leading to the affected villages were closed by police, while officers launched a large-scale operation to find the suspect.
The newspaper Milliyet reported that a vehicle allegedly taken by the attacker had been later found stuck in mud - the suspect having abandoned it before fleeing on foot.

In a statement posted on social media, the Afyonkarahisar Governorate said "all relevant institutions of our state have been working in coordination since the very first moment and are meticulously carrying out the necessary work".

articles.headline: Melania Trump calls for peace at meeting with Russia, Ukraine officials
keyFacts: US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukraine officials at the White House to urge a lasting peace after a recent localized ceasefire.
The expired six-day truce allowed aid deliveries and evacuations in Oleshky, marking the longest multi-day truce since the 2022 invasion.
New US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.
body: United States First Lady Melania Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine to build on a recent localised ceasefire and seek a more “enduring” peace, as she hosted officials from both countries at the White House.

Melania Trump spoke on Thursday at an event that the White House said is believed to be “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.

Those attending included Kirill Dmitriev, a special envoy of Russian President Vladimir Putin; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” Mrs. Trump said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.

She said her role as “exclusive intermediary” was set out in written agreements signed by both countries, and that she was involved in every stage of the planning, including reviewing de-mining plans and evacuation routes.

Ukrainian representatives presented the US first lady with the Order of Princess Olga, first class, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy awarded her earlier this week. She also gave the most senior officials present letters she had written to Putin and Zelenskyy.
The six-day truce covered the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region and the surrounding area, and allowed aid deliveries and the evacuation of nearly 800 people.

An estimated 2,000 civilians had been left in the city. It was the longest multi-day truce between Russia and Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the first joint relief operation in four years and eight months.
The White House said Melania Trump mediated the truce, though Pope Leo XIV also pressed both sides to allow aid and evacuations, and that the two accounts of who brokered it have diverged.

The truce expired last Sunday with no extension, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region, killed at least 40 people, according to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy.
New US-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11.

articles.headline: The Democrats have a Christianity problem — Trump’s GOP is just as lost
keyFacts: The author states that several newly elected Democratic ministers and seminarians reject core Christian doctrines regarding salvation and biblical authority.
The author criticizes specific Democrats, such as Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III, for controversial statements and associations.
The author argues that right-wing political figures, including Donald Trump, also promote unbiblical views and a shallow version of Christianity.
body: The Left may be on the rise, but the Democratic Party has a Christianity problem. In taking home a landslide midterm victory on Tuesday, the Democrats elected five ministers and a seminarian. The problem: I’m not exactly sure I’d use the term “Christian” to describe them.

Sens.-elect James Talarico (D-TX) and Adam Hamilton (D-KS) and Rep.-elect Lindsay James (D-IA) are the most egregious examples, as they reject the core Christian doctrine that Jesus Christ is the only way to eternal life. This is such a central tenet of Christianity that I could not in good faith refer to them as my “brothers/sister in Christ.”

Talarico has said that all religions have the “same truth” and claims salvation is earned by feeding the hungry, helping the sick, welcoming strangers, and visiting prisoners. Hamilton has said that those who did not place their faith in the Lord Jesus Christ during their life will still go to heaven. James belongs to a denomination whose doctrinal statement says it doesn’t “restrict the grace of God to those who profess explicit faith in Christ.”
BELTWAY CONFIDENTIAL— YES, JD VANCE: LOSING THE MIDTERMS WAS ‘WORTH IT’ TO PREVENT A NUCLEAR IRAN

The Bible , however, says that anyone preaching a false gospel like the ones mentioned above is “accursed” — or on their way to hell, in other words (Galatians 1:8-9). There is only one gospel by which a sinner can receive salvation, according to the very Bible which these professing Christians claim to preach.

The word “gospel” means “good news.” And paired with good news, as often is the case, is bad news. The bad news is that every one of us is a sinner (Romans 3:23), and our sin earns us an eternity in hell (Romans 6:23) that we cannot earn our way out of (Galatians 2:21). But the good news is that Jesus Christ, who is God in the flesh, came down from heaven to die on the cross and shed his blood to pay for our sins (Romans 3:25), was buried, and rose from the dead (1 Corinthians 15:1-4). Because God sees our righteousness “as filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6),” we must receive Jesus’s righteousness to be saved. To do so, you must put your trust in his blood atonement and ask him to save you from your sins (Romans 10:9-10).

This isn’t some complicated or hidden idea. It’s literally the very foundation of Christianity. One does not become a Christian until they have received the above gospel. So how is it possible that two ministers and a seminarian don’t know this? Hamilton has the answer.

Less than 60 seconds before saying in a sermon that non-Christians go to heaven despite rejecting the gospel, Hamilton said that God “didn’t give us a book.” Mind you, he was standing right in front of an open Bible! One can only assume it was for decoration, because if he had ever opened it, he would have read that not only did God give us a book, but also that Psalm 138:2 says God has “magnified thy word above all thy name.” And Isaiah 34:16 says, “Seek ye out of the book of the Lord, and read.”

So that explains a lot. It also explains how James, as well as Reps.-elect LaKesha Womack (D-NC) and Sarah Trone Garriott (D-IA) decided to become ministers despite the Bible’s explicit prohibition on female ministers in 1 Timothy 2:11-14, 1 Corinthians 14:34-35, 1 Timothy 3:1-12, and Titus 1:5-6. The latter congresswoman-elect has also defended and facilitated non-Christian public prayers (including Wiccan/pagan and Muslim) in the Iowa Capitol/Senate and officiated a wedding for a couple who literally identified as Satanists — because of course she did.

The sixth and final current-or-future clergy member heading to Capitol Hill for the Democrats is Rep.-elect Frederick Haynes III (D-TX), and he’s in a woke category of his own. While other Democrats like Talarico are woke in the sense that they apologize for being white, claim “God is non-binary,” and obsess over “trans children,” Haynes is a militant black nationalist who gushes over former Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan as “a wonderful and great man.”

Farrakhan notoriously said “Hitler was a very great man,” blamed “bloodsucking” Jews for the Holocaust and 9/11, referred to Jews as “termites,” chanted “death to Israel,” said that “white people are potential humans [who] haven’t evolved yet,” and engaged in so much more vile rhetoric you could fill multiple volumes. And in pure Farrakhan fashion, on the Sunday after Charlie Kirk was killed, Haynes took to the pulpit to push the idea that Kirk was “not assassinated” and that his death shouldn’t be described in the same manner as black civil rights leaders who suffered the same fate. He also lambasted the “white Christian” as a “hate-filled” racist and white supremacist. And the very day after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023 terrorist attack in which over 1,000 Jews were murdered, tortured, maimed, raped, and kidnapped, Haynes spent his sermon slandering the victims as members of an apartheid state. Not to mention, he rallied behind convicted murderer Karmelo Anthony , whom he referred to as “our friend,” after he stabbed a 17-year-old white child to death.
So this is the current state of so-called “Christianity” in the Democratic Party. But is the Republican Party faring much better?

While there do appear to be some Bible-believing members of the GOP, the kind of Christianity being promoted by right-wing figures is shallow at best and apostate at worst. President Donald Trump , for example, has said that he’s trying to get into heaven by negotiating peace deals on Earth. If I could show the president one verse, it would be this: “Every man at his best state is altogether vanity” (Psalm 39:5). No matter who you are, two things are true: every man will die someday, and every man will be judged (Hebrews 9:27). Your very best is not good enough to overcome your sins — only the blood of Christ, which must be received by faith , can wash them away.

So apart from the wokeness, Trump is just as bad as the Democrats on this matter. But it gets worse, because the people in Trump’s orbit, such as charismatic female pastor Paula White, are making the president out to be a messianic figure with a divine decree from God to impose his agenda on the country. War Secretary Pete Hegseth even portrayed Trump as Jesus in an analogy comparing the president’s critics to Pharisees.

We’re also seeing “Christian” celebrities flock to the Right; the Turning Point USA types. One must look no further than Kid Rock , who just released a new so-called “Christian” album last month. This is what he has to say about his faith: “I didn’t get saved. I’m still Kid Rock. I’ll drink a beer, smoke a cigar … I feel like I’ve always been right with God.”
BELTWAY CONFIDENTIAL — OBAMA IS ‘TIRED OF BEING DIVIDED’: POT, MEET KETTLE

The Bible says that if you’re not saved, you are not right with God. Rather, “the wrath of God abideth on him” (John 3:36). And the idea that drinking a beer or smoking a cigar, which admittedly no Christian should do, precludes you from salvation is completely unbiblical. Even after you receive the gospel, you will never achieve sinless perfection while “in the body of this death” (Romans 7:24). The big takeaway: Many of these professing Christians on the Right are just as lost as the professing Christians on the Left. MAGA Christianity, as it appears, is not substantially different from the Left’s version of Christianity, apart from the wokeness.

Left-wing “Christianity” is “peace, love, inclusion” — right-wing “Christianity” is “freedom, guns, ‘merica.” But Jesus Christ is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). Political figures on both sides say they believe this, but their own words and actions betray them.

articles.headline: White House Twitter account faceplants with awful Zelda AI slop that missed the midterms by two days
keyFacts: The White House Twitter account posted an AI-generated video featuring Donald Trump in a style inspired by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
The video was released two days after the Republican Party suffered a defeat in the midterm elections.
The content features an AI-generated version of Donald Trump running through a corridor while listing his presidential achievements.
body: Donald Trump’s staff apparently loves games, especially that one where we play as that boy Zelda, so they released a self-endorsement Ocarina of Time -inspired AI slop video to accompany the release of the game’s eagerly anticipated remaster.
It's dangerous to go alone! Take this 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/masCWWQe7m
— The White House (@WhiteHouse) November 5, 2026

It’s embarrassing for many reasons. First off, it’s impossible to ignore how this is one of the first official statements coming out of the White House after the Republican Party’s heavy defeat in the midterm elections.

Then, there’s how the iconic red hat that once bravely displayed the infamous message about making America great again has been replaced by one that says “Still your President”. For the first time in a while, it feels less like a threat, more like a desperate reminder.

Image via x.com/WhiteHouse (Editor’s note: how is this timeline real?) It’s surprisingly boring, too, just showing Trump running through a never-ending corridor in an attempt to reach the Deku tree while listing a bunch of his supposed achievements in office. And even though this was clearly meant to ride the remaster’s coattails, it doesn’t even show the new graphics, opting instead for a weird AI Trumpified version of the old ones.

It gives the ick—a relatively new expression used to describe the moment when all the attraction you feel for a prospective love interest dies immediately because of something random they do. People in politics have been talking for a while about simple actions that immediately killed a candidate’s credibility: when Nixon supposedly lost the election to Kennedy because he was sweating too profusely during a debate, when Howard Dean supposedly lost his bid for the White House because he let out a silly-sounding scream during a celebration, or when Hillary Clinton told us all to Pokémon Go to the polls. I don’t know about all the previous ones, but I remember feeling right there and then that Hillary was toast.

And I just can’t help but feel like Trump pulling this after such a massive defeat feels like his own “ Pokémon Go to the polls” moment, or, should I say, his “ Ocarina of Time ” to go to the polls. I know it’s actually too late for that, but doesn’t that make it even more on-brand?

articles.headline: Ablahshikar is a maximalist, sickos only salvage-survival CRPG about ripping organs out of warships and pawning off strange goods that's now out in early access
keyFacts: The turn-based salvage-survival CRPG Ablahshikar has launched in early access on Steam.
Players pilot ancient ships and harvest organs from enemy warships to rebuild their own vessels.
The game will remain in early access for approximately two months before the price increases.
body: Sometimes, you come across a game and instantly know it's for the sickos. Today that is Ablahshikar, a "turn-based salvage-survival CRPG adrift on the Candle Sea" where you rip out the organs of enemy warships to "rebuild your vessel into a doomed chimera," that is out now in early access. To be honest I could have just called it a CRPG and still labelled it as a game for sickos, yet everything that's going on here is obviously just doubling down on the sick factor.

Ablahshikar is a particular flavour of maximalism. Having not played it, it feels a bit impossible describe, I mean, just have a read of some of the game's Steam page: "Lo, destiny crooks a finger only to those whose eyes peer beyond þe next tempest. Take custody of a faltering war-barge that wanders the outer brine of Dastgerd. Thy wrists y-braced to a wan terminal of bone-whyte and tarnysshed latoun, þou steerest Ablahshikar by murke point-nettes and sputteryng tables." I don't know what any of that means! And I love it. Reminds me of Hylics in that the game's world is not translating itself for its audience; you take what you're given, and you figure it out yourself.

Judging from trailers and screenshots, there's a mix of activities to be getting on with. Occasionally you'll be piloting a strange, not alien, but definitely ancient ship of some kind in an arcadey sort of fashion. Then occasionally there's something that resembles Caves of Qud, i.e. some odd, 2D maybe dungeon crawling where your moves are dictated by individual keys on your keyboard. Then there's Disco Elysiumy cutscenes that feel like a video game designed in the year 1200 by someone from the year 2200, aesthetically anyway. As I said, it is a particular flavour of maximalism.

Truthfully, I do not know if I am sicko enough for Ablahshikar. Its mighty vision is terrifying, but I certainly am curious about it. Right now it's less than a fiver, and it'll only be in early access for roughly a couple of months where the price will then go up, so perhaps it's best to get in at the ground floor. If you are one such sicko, then you can pick it up on Steam right here.

articles.headline: Is MAHA dying—or will it be reborn? What's next after crushing midterm losses?
keyFacts: The Make America Health Again movement faced significant losses in the recent midterm elections.
Supporters are questioning the movement's future after internal divisions and electoral defeats.
Activist Mary Talley Bowden is polling followers on whether to form a third party or target the GOP.
body: As Democrats blew away their Republican rivals in an unprecedented midterm sweep Tuesday, the Make America Health Again movement also got bowled over, raising questions about the fate of the motley movement.

MAHA—which has centered around anti-vaccine activist and current Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.—saw many of its favored candidates and allies lose, while vocal adversaries of Kennedy won. And the coalition was splintering under stress even before the voting started; in recent months, supporters have accused Kennedy and the Trump administration of inaction and betrayals in their two years in power.

Now hobbled in Washington, shedding supporters, and showing little to no influence in voting booths, is MAHA on its deathbed? Or will it be reborn—possibly into a new group? Could it be assimilated into a blue platform—after sloughing off the more repulsive, conspiratorial aspects of Kennedy’s ideology? These are the questions circling in the aftermath of Tuesday’s bloodbath.

In a social media poll Wednesday afternoon, Mary Talley Bowden—a dejected MAHA activist, anti-vaccine advocate, and doctor reprimanded for prescribing ivermectin to treat COVID-19—polled her followers about what should come next. She offered three options: Start a third party, join the Democrats, or overthrow the GOP. As of publication time, joining Democrats trailed at just 3 percent of the votes. The remaining votes were roughly split between overthrowing the GOP—whatever that means—and forming a third party, which had a small lead at 49 percent.
Cracking coalition

That MAHA could fade out entirely or fracture into negligible shards seems like a very real possibility. Its collection of disparate groups and varied agenda items has always made its cohesiveness seem tenuous. A Politico poll in June revealed that people who identified as MAHA had different ideas of what the movement’s priorities are (or should be), as well as different political leanings, and sometimes opposing ideologies.
