articles.headline: HR thinks you can learn AI skills – so why is your company hiring elsewhere?
keyFacts: Most HR professionals and managers believe current employees can be reskilled for AI roles, according to a Careerminds study.
Organizations frequently hire externally for AI positions instead of redeploying existing staff due to difficulties in tracking internal skill sets.
External hiring for AI roles is often more expensive and time-consuming than training current employees, according to research cited in the report.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- HR sees AI reskilling potential, but outside hiring outpaces internal moves.
- Limited visibility into AI skills makes reskilling opportunities hard to spot.
- Hiring externally often costs more and takes longer than reskilling.
HR leaders are confident that current employees can be trained for jobs created by artificial intelligence. Organizations are hiring externally instead.

That’s the finding in new research from Careerminds, a global provider of workforce solutions. The study, published in Careerminds’ white paper, The AI Redeployment Gap: What Companies Lose by Hiring over Reskilling, reveals that 92% of HR professionals and 88% of people managers believe employees within their organizations could be reskilled for AI-related roles.
More from ZDNET

Yet 51% of HR professionals and 47% of people managers report that their organizations are hiring externally for new AI-related positions, compared with just 42% in each group who report redeploying existing employees.

The research was conducted in partnership with Censuswide and surveyed 595 US HR professionals and 547 US people managers, ages 25–65, working at organizations with 500-10,000 or more employees. The research was conducted May 15–26, 2026.

“Companies are investing in AI while potentially overlooking one of their most valuable resources: the people they already employ,” said Mark Saddic, senior partner at Careerminds, in a press release.
Why companies struggle to identify employees for AI reskilling

Reskilling, especially for AI, isn’t easy to track. Limited visibility into individual skill sets and which employees should be reskilled was cited as a potential barrier by 43% of HR professionals and 34% of managers.

It’s not the first time that the management of skills development has come up regarding AI. In September, educational giant Pearson agreed to acquire Workera, the AI-native skills platform used by organizations such as ServiceNow, Accenture, and the US Space Force.

Careermind’s data revealed that 87% of HR pros and 84% of managers believe their organizations are adequately considering reskilling employees for future roles. However, the findings suggest that these organizations may believe they are prioritizing internal talent development, even though their hiring practices reveal otherwise.
How AI hiring and reskilling differ by industry
Response to AI-related workforce needs isn’t equal across the board. The findings reveal significant differences in how industries are responding to these needs.

For example, in the technology and telecom industries, external hiring outpaces redeployment by 15%. At the same time, media and entertainment is the only sector surveyed in which both groups report redeployment at least as frequently as external hiring. Among HR professionals in that industry, 56% report redeploying employees, compared with just 25% who hire externally.
And this divide is costly, too.
External hiring cost more than filling roles internally

Separate research from The Josh Bersin Company, cited in the Careerminds white paper, reveals that external hiring can cost three to five times more than filling comparable roles internally — and on average takes up to 20 days longer.

articles.headline: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
keyFacts: Paraguay's lower house voted unanimously to impeach President Santiago Peña minutes after he resigned following the collapse of Ueno Bank.

The Senate will vote on whether to convict Peña, while Vice President Pedro Alliana is expected to be sworn in to serve out the remainder of the term.
body: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguay's lower house voted unanimously Thursday to impeach President Santiago Peña just minutes after he announced his resignation, as the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings, sent protesters surging into the streets and turned his own party against him.

The 78-0 vote marked a stunning repudiation of Peña by lawmakers from his long-ruling Colorado Party, who joined the opposition in backing his impeachment after three days of demonstrations rocked the capital, Asunción. The vote sends the charges to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is required to convict the president and formally remove him from office.
The impeachment came as thousands protested for a third day, as they attempt to recoup lost savings, wages and pensions from Ueno Bank, a major digital lender.

Peña, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

The president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.
"I also want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."

The extraordinary turn of events set the stage for a transfer of power later Thursday. Congress was expected to formally accept Peña's resignation at 5 p.m., clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in as president an hour later. Alliana would serve out Peña's term through August 2028, with lawmakers expected to choose a new vice president.
From star lender to seized bank

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.

Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno's holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left.

Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña's request.

Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.
Protesters in the streets

Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank's parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.

"We want your head, Peña!" they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña's impeachment, called him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.

Many demonstrators saw Ueno's collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.
"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said protester Belarmino Balbuena.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.

articles.headline: The moment Donald Trump blew the midterms
keyFacts: Democrats won a large midterm victory, capturing over 250 House seats and flipping several Republican strongholds.
Data scientist David Shor said the surge was driven by high turnout among young, Latino, and politically disengaged voters.
Shor noted that President Donald Trump lost public trust on the economy following the Iran war.
body: President Donald Trump arrives on stage to deliver remarks during an election rally at McMorran Place Sports & Entertainment Center on October 25, 2026, in Port Huron, Michigan. | Alex Wong/Getty Images

Democrats just partied like it’s 1974. On Tuesday night, they pulled off the largest midterm victory since the post-Watergate wave. Democratic Senate candidates conquered longtime Republican strongholds like Kansas and Texas — and probably (in the view of the internet’s gamblers) Mississippi and Alaska . When the dust settles, and all ballots are tallied, Democrats are expected to boast a 13-percentage-point popular vote victory and more than 250 House seats.
Taken together, these results exceeded many Democrats’ wildest dreams — and Republicans’ greatest fears. Countless Americans are therefore asking: How the hell did that happen?

To make some headway on that question, I spoke with the Democratic data scientist David Shor. Founder of the consultancy Blue Rose Research, Shor has access to volumes of large-sample polling, precinct-level data on which voters did (and did not) turn out in multiple states, and fine-grained estimates of demographic shifts in party allegiances.

Historically, Shor has been one of the Democrats’ most prominent Cassandras . For years, he has warned that his party’s falling support among working-class voters threatened to make Democratic Senate majorities a thing of the past.
Key takeaways
Democratic turnout surged, particularly among young, politically disengaged, and Latino voters.
The Iran war was President Donald Trump’s downfall.
Campaign donors have weird priorities and issue positions, which can undermine politicians who take their money.
Polling is getting harder.
Americans think AI might take their jobs and kill their families.
So, I wanted to ask him about the story that his numbers are now telling — and whether it challenges his past assumptions about how American politics works.

On Wednesday afternoon, we also discussed shifts in youth turnout, why Elon Musk’s money bought Republicans so little, and Americans’ growing contempt for artificial intelligence, among other things. Our conversation has been edited for clarity and length.
What happened Tuesday night? How did Democrats end up with the biggest landslide in half a century?

It’s early; a lot of precincts haven’t come in and we only have individual-level data in a couple of places. But Democrats appear to be running about 7 points ahead of where Kamala Harris was [in 2024].

And it seems like a very large portion of that was due to turnout. You can see this in both the precinct and county-level data. But we also have data on individual voters in Texas and Georgia. And in those two places, Harris supporters turned out at a rate about 9 points higher than Trump supporters did. That’s likely the largest turnout advantage going back to at least 2006. For context, the gap in 2018 was about 3 points.

And a lot of that was young voters. It’s funny; in 2022, everyone said there was a “ youthquake ” — a huge spike in youth turnout — which was overstated. But this time, one genuinely happened. In Georgia and Texas, there was an enormous increase in youth turnout and actual declines in turnout among voters over 65.

We also have evidence that Democrats gained ground with politically disengaged voters. In the precincts that had the lowest turnout rates in 2022, Democrats gained something like 11 points. Whereas the highest turnout precincts swung toward us by only 2 or 3 points.

It’s a little hard to distinguish changes in support from changes in turnout. But it’s clear that young voters, Hispanic voters, and infrequent voters swung toward us, reversing much of the gains that Republicans made with those groups in 2024.
How big was the increase in Black turnout? Looking at Democrats’ remarkable success in South Carolina and Mississippi , it seems like African American mobilization must have been a factor.

In the Georgia data, we see a 4-percentage-point increase in the Black share of the electorate relative to 2022, which is quite a bit. And in Texas, we see a nearly 6-percentage-point increase in the Latino share of the electorate.
What explains these shifts in turnout and voting patterns?

If you look at Trump approval — both from 2016 to 2020 and then from 2024 until the end of 2025 — it was really quite stable. Obviously, it was highest at the beginning of his terms and went down after a month or two. But then for most of Trump’s first term, he was hovering around the mid-40s in our data and it really barely moved in response to events. And it was much the same for the first year of Trump’s second term. Which was worrisome: Trump had all of these scandals, but at the end of the day, the line didn’t move. A good day would be like, “Oh, Trump approval is down three-tenths of a percentage point — amazing!”
So, a lot of people became very nihilistic. They were like, “Oh, we really live in this world where nothing matters.”

But then, the Iran war happened. And there was a giant structural shift in public opinion. His approval rating on the cost of living plummeted. To put some numbers on this, the day before the Iran war, Donald Trump had a 49 percent approval rating on gas prices. Within a week, it was 33 percent.

Trump’s overall approval rating isn’t that much lower than in 2018. And his approval on immigration, healthcare, and a lot of other issues is pretty similar. The big change in our polling has been a giant decline in Trump’s approval on the economy.

And previously, voters’ trust in his economic management was the one thing propping him up. But the Iran war destroyed it. And he went from being a complicated political figure — who was popular on the economy but unpopular on other things — to being unpopular on everything.

So, Tuesday’s wave had less to do with what Democrats did right than what Republicans did wrong? Are there portable lessons here for Democrats besides, “When a GOP president engineers a massive increase in gas prices, tell voters you disapprove?”

I’m not going to claim that the Democratic brand is perfect. But I think the Democratic leadership and both wings of the Democratic Party — the left and the “establishment” or whatever — deserve a lot of credit for making big, concrete shifts in their messaging; specifically, focusing more on economic issues that affect people’s everyday lives. That was not a given. It was not uncontroversial at the time. And it paid dividends.

Right before the 2024 election, Republicans had a 12-point trust advantage on the cost of living. Today, among 2026 voters, Democrats actually have the trust advantage on the issue, which continues to be voters’ No. 1 concern by far.

We ask voters questions like, “What do you think the Democratic Party cares about?” And when we asked that question a year after the 2024 election, voters thought Democrats prioritized catering to their base over the cost of living by 4 to 1.

When we ran that survey again right before this year’s election, voters thought Democrats cared about the cost of living more than anything else, just like them. They thought Democrats’ second concern was fighting Donald Trump, which maybe wasn’t a total positive. But then No. 3 was healthcare and No. 4 was the economy. And so Democrats really did execute a big pivot.

And meanwhile, if you ask voters what they think that Trump cares about, they say border security, immigration, national security, and war in the Middle East. You have to go far down the list to get to costs.
The other thing I’d say for Democratic strategy: The 2025 government shutdown did damage Trump.

Until then, Trump really felt like he had escalation dominance, that basically every time he would violate norms and trigger a fight, he felt — based on previous experience — that he would win and that Democrats would have to back down. And this was the first high-profile fight between Democrats and Trump where he really paid a big price and his approval started to go down.

And I think that partly reflects Democrats choosing to center the shutdown on healthcare, one of the issues voters really cared about. There were a lot of people in the Democratic Party who wanted to focus on other things, for understandable reasons. But if you look at the postmortem, the healthcare shutdown corresponded with a massive increase in the salience of healthcare in the minds of voters. And that correspondingly led to an increase in support for Democrats and disapproval of Trump.
In our past conversations , you often painted a pretty bleak picture of the Democratic Party’s prospects for winning control of the Senate. And not without reason.

In the last few elections, it seemed like moderate Democratic candidates were having a harder and harder time competing in Republican-leaning states. Which was a problem, since Democrats couldn’t win control of the Senate without prevailing in states that voted for Trump every chance they got.

And you argued that Democrats’ problem was structural: Voters increasingly got their political information from national outlets, which focused on the big-picture ideological divides between the two parties rather than the idiosyncratic positioning of individual candidates. Culturally conservative Montana voters realized that voting for Jon Tester meant empowering social liberals. And so Democrats were kind of screwed, unless they found a way to moderate their national image.

And yet, the national Democratic Party didn’t really moderate any of its issue positions between 2024 and 2026 — yet still managed to win statewide elections in Kansas, Iowa, and probably Alaska and Mississippi. So, how do you reconcile these results with your model of political reality?

I’m a little more wary of making long-term predictions than I was in my 20s. Obviously, I would have been shocked in 2019 if you had told me how many Senate seats we would have today. But it’s worth walking through what happened, year by year.

What’s interesting about 2022 and 2024 is that we really should have lost a lot of races, in many different senses. What saved us is that, in both those years, Democrats had a historic advantage in candidate quality — measured by objective things like, “Was this person elected to a previous office?”
And if you really drill into individual details, this was largely because Trump intervened in swing-state primaries in the House and Senate to support lower-quality candidates who were loyal to him.

One mathematical way to see this is to look at how Democrats in swing races did relative to Democrats in non-swing races. And in 2014 and 2018, the gap was basically zero. But in 2022, it was something like 3 percent. And then in 2024, it was a little bit more muted, but similar.

So, I think Republicans were on the cusp of securing a level of power in American politics that no party had experienced in decades. But Trump spent down that power to accomplish his goals. I definitely didn’t see that coming.
As for this election, I did not predict that Trump would start a super unpopular war while also doing massive tariffs and making a bunch of other domestic political miscalculations.

I have two takeaways from all this. The first is I think that political parties have a real tendency towards equilibrating behavior, where in response to having lots of seats, they go and do a bunch of politically counterproductive things.
The other piece is: In the past, I had said that it was impossible to hold the Senate without Democrats winning culturally conservative voters in states that backed Trump by large margins.

And that continues to be true. The question was, “Is it possible for us to get there?” At the time, I think a lot of people really thought that these levels of overperformance were impossible. But it turns out there are different paths to getting there, and one is having the president launch a giant unpopular war, while doing everything he can to drive down his own approval rating.

What do you think this election tells us about the power of money in politics? The GOP had a financial advantage this cycle. And yet, at first glance, it doesn’t look like Elon Musk’s $445 million investment in Republican power made much of a difference.

Obviously money does matter. Ads do work. It’s not like these effects are zero . But as the amount of money in politics has increased, political parties have started catering enormously to the whims of donors who are really quite weird.

In our issue priorities polling, the cost of living is the top issue for every subgroup imaginable — young voters, Hispanic voters, Black voters, old voters, whatever. Every single group, except for the 0.7 percent of the population that has donated to a Democratic campaign in the last year. And for them, climate change is No. 1, voting rights is No. 2, you have to go down to like 11 or something to get to the cost of living. And I think that explains a lot about elite Democrats’ behavior historically.
So, it’s better to be outspent and in touch with the American voter than it is to be the opposite. I like to say: Whichever party listens less to their donors usually wins.

You can’t blame donors for everything in the Trump presidency — tariffs were probably all him — but if you look at what he did, his donors pushed him to take incredibly unpopular positions on AI and on data centers.
“In our issue priorities polling, the cost of living is the top issue for every subgroup imaginable — young voters, Hispanic voters, Black voters, old voters, whatever.”

After Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic , Trump said that no new AI regulations were needed. We polled that statement. And it was literally the most unpopular position I’ve ever seen a mainstream politician endorse. About 8 percent of people supported it. That’s three times less popular than defunding the police.

Holding all else equal, more money is helpful. But if getting it requires you to spend 70 to 80 percent of your time talking to some of the weirdest people on the planet — and forces you to prioritize issues that the general public doesn’t care about — you’re better off with less money.

Zohran Mamdani is an example of this. He showed that if you single-mindedly focus your campaign on voters’ top issue — affordability — you can really do incredible things, while your opponents are wasting time arguing about Israel.

Why did the polls underestimate Democrats so significantly? In some recent elections, polls had tended to overestimate Democrats , particularly in redder areas. And you argued this was because voters with low social trust had become both less likely to answer a pollster’s call — and more likely to support Republicans. And that led pollsters to systematically undercount Trump voters. But this time, the miss went in the other direction.

We’re still trying to piece together exactly what the data says. But the fundamental problem in polling is that the two biggest predictors of answering a phone survey are: 1) how interested you are in politics and 2) your socioeconomic status — as measured not only by education and income, but also things that are much harder for survey takers to gauge, like, “How educated were your parents?” or “What’s the occupational prestige of your job?” or “What kind of neighborhood do you live in?”
In 2012, a voter’s level of interest in politics wasn’t super correlated with support for Obama or Romney. But now they are.

And technology is part of why. If you go back to the 1950s, if someone received a call from a pollster, they’d be like, “Oh my God, there’s a researcher who wants to know my views on contemporary events!” and they would excitedly drop what they’re doing and talk to them. But now there is a multitrillion-dollar war for people’s attention. And so it is in fact quite hard to get non-random samples of people excited to take that call. That problem isn’t going away. So I expect more polling misses in the future.

How do you interpret the variation in Democratic performance between states? Democratic Senate candidates in Texas and Iowa vastly outperformed Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins, while those in Maine and Michigan did so more modestly. How much of that gap is driven by demographics — Trump simply induced a backlash among specific groups that are more present in some states than in others — versus candidate quality? And to the extent that candidate quality was important, did that boil down to ideological positioning or more intangible assets?

We did a big survey right before the election where we asked voters, “How moderate do you think this candidate is?” And then we also asked a bunch of other questions like, “How much do you think this person cares about economic issues?” “How in touch are they with the economic struggles that everyday people face?”

And we found that perceived moderation is associated with higher vote share. Though I think in the House, these effects are smaller than a lot of people would guess. What’s more interesting, though, is it really seems like the extent to which voters see you as focused on economic issues — and in touch with what regular people care about — is much more predictive of overperformance than ideology.
And I think that if you go and look at individual politicians, there are lots of examples of both progressive and moderate politicians who are perceived as out of touch.

And I think the left is learning this. If you look at the ideological penalty that candidates supported by Justice Democrats have paid each election cycle, they’ve gone down over time, as these groups have matured a bit and focused on economic messaging.

One big story from Tuesday night was the massive backlash to data center construction. Forty out of 41 ballot proposals for restricting data centers passed. What do you make of that? In your polling, is this opposition driven primarily by concerns about the structures themselves — their appearance, pollution, and impact on local energy bills? Or is it primarily an outlet for voters to express their antipathy for AI as a technology?

Over the last two years, voters have grown increasingly concerned about AI. In 2024, AI ranked 40th out of 40 on our list of voter priorities. But it’s gained salience by more than any other issue since the start of Trump’s presidency; now it’s ranked 24th out of 39, roughly tied with crime.

And as that salience has increased, people have become increasingly negative about AI. In December of last year, we asked people whether they were more optimistic or pessimistic about AI, and optimism led by about 5 points. In our most recent polling, pessimism leads by 10 points.

Late last year, when we asked, “Do you want a data center built in your neighborhood?” we saw 45 percent support. In our polling a month or two ago, that fell to 14 percent. For context, when you ask voters whether they want a prison in their neighborhood, that figure is 15 percent.
And obviously, part of that is NIMBY concerns. But I think that this is part and parcel of AI becoming more unpopular.

And I think it’s impossible to understand why AI is unpopular without considering voters’ views on the broader economy. Consumer confidence is roughly at the level it was right after the Great Recession. Ask people, “Do you think the economy is rigged for elites or are things fair?” People say “rigged.” Ask, “Do you trust our business elites?” People overwhelmingly say no. And these are very big changes from before the pandemic.

So, if you believe the country’s elites cannot be trusted — and then you also hear a bunch of business people saying, “AI is going to change everything!” — it’s natural to assume that change is going to screw you.

And in fact, 80 percent of voters say it’s either very likely or somewhat likely that there will be large-scale job loss due to AI in the next five years. And something like 64 percent say it’s either very likely or somewhat likely that AI will threaten human survival. So the median voter thinks that there is a considerable chance that AI will take their job and kill their family.

If America’s tech elites really want this large-scale build out and reorganization of the economy to happen, they will have to actually pressure Congress to meaningfully protect the downside risks of the American people and guarantee them some share of AI’s upside. Because, as we saw yesterday, we live in a democracy. And the American people will not allow this AI transition to happen unless they get something for it.

articles.headline: Get root on a musl Linux system by slamming it with an overly long password
keyFacts: Researcher Özgün Kültekin discovered a vulnerability allowing root access on certain Linux systems using musl libc by entering passwords longer than 256 bytes.
The flaw affects systems running OpenSSH without Pluggable Authentication Modules where password authentication is enabled and specific account configurations exist.
OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 to fix the issue, and users can alternatively disable password authentication to protect their systems.
body: On certain Linux systems, an attacker could gain root access by entering a password longer than 256 bytes. The vulnerability, dubbed *sshole by Wakefield researcher Özgün Kültekin, who discovered it, can only be exploited in very specific conditions.

The flaw affects certain Linux systems using musl libc instead of the traditional GNU C library, and even then only those running OpenSSH's secure shell daemon without Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) and with password authentication enabled.

If those conditions are met, and at least one other account has a valid password hash, accounts that shouldn't accept passwords, such as root, key-only deployment users, and LDAP users, may be accessed by supplying a password between 257 and 1,024 characters. The targeted accounts must have an asterisk (*) in their password field, and direct root login remains subject to OpenSSH's configuration.
That might seem niche, but sorry: It’s not.

Musl libc is common in embedded Linux systems due to its low footprint. More critically than that, it's also the standard C library for Alpine Linux, which provides official cloud images for both AWS and Azure. Some Alpine systems running in those environments may therefore be vulnerable, depending on their configuration.
Dawn of the *sshole
The vulnerability in OpenSSH on musl-based Linux systems dates back to 2016, but Kültekin explains that its roots go back much further – to the BSD Unix era, actually.

In 1980, Sun Microsystems cofounder and BSD Unix heavyweight Bill Joy was involved in the development of BSD Unix, whose password file contained a single asterisk in the /etc/passwd entry for the daemon user. The asterisk wasn't a password hash and effectively disabled password authentication for that account.

Nowadays, password hashes typically live in /etc/shadow and contain hashed information that the system uses to verify a plaintext password entered by a user. Asterisks are still present for accounts that aren't supposed to accept password logins, but as Kültekin explains in his writeup, that isn't exactly a foolproof way to keep people out.

The crypt() function, which generates password hashes for comparison with stored values, can return NULL if it can't compute a hash. Applications that fail to check that result may crash. Musl libc's developers instead chose to return a single character for certain failures, and they picked the asterisk.

Musl also added SHA-512-based password hashing around the same time, which Kültekin notes gets slower the longer a password is, potentially leading to denial of service if someone floods a server with a super-long password. Musl capped passwords at 256 bytes, and you can likely see where this is going.

In 2016, OpenSSH introduced a workaround to prevent attackers from enumerating valid account names through SSH. Before the change, sshd could reject authentication attempts for nonexistent users more quickly than those for valid accounts. Attempts against valid accounts took longer because the server had to hash the supplied password before rejecting it. The solution was to have sshd perform dummy password hashing for invalid users, using an appropriate hashing algorithm and salt to reduce differences in response times.

On affected musl-based Linux systems, accounts marked with an asterisk instead of a password hash could be busted open by supplying a password longer than 256 bytes – a flaw dating back to 2016. Any musl-based Linux system running a vulnerable OpenSSH configuration without PAM, with password authentication enabled, at least one account marked with an asterisk, and another account with a valid password hash could be vulnerable to a *sshole attack.

Luckily, OpenSSH acted fast to fix this issue , and any OpenSSH build 10.6p2 (released Thursday) or newer is protected. Alternatively, if you can’t update your OpenSSH implementation on an affected system, just disable password authentication and restart the SSH daemon and you should be all set.

There’s no indication that vulnerable systems have been exploited, but if you want to check, Kültekin has included a simple CLI command in his writeup that can be used to check if any no-password accounts on a sensitive machine recently took a password. ®

articles.headline: The SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro Wireless Gaming Headset With Infinite Battery Life Drops to a New Low
keyFacts: Woot is selling the SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro wireless gaming headset for $183.99 using the coupon code PCGAMING.
The headset features a hot-swappable battery system that allows for continuous use by charging one battery while the other is in the device.
This deal includes a brand new headset with a 90-day Woot warranty and free shipping for Amazon Prime members.
body: One of the best wireless gaming headsets just dropped to its lowest price ever. Woot, which is owned by Amazon, is offering a new Steelseries Arctis Nova Pro wireless gaming headset for PS5, PS4, and PC for just $183.99 after you apply 20% off coupon code " PCGAMING ". Amazon Prime members get free shipping, otherwise add $5 for delivery. This is a brand new, unused headset that comes with a 90-day Woot warranty.
SteelSeries Nova Pro Wireless Gaming Headset for $184

The SteelSeries Arctis Nova Pro has long been one of IGN's highest rated wireless gaming headsets . IGN's Kevin Lee gave the Nova Pro a 10/10 "Masterpiece" review and I believe it still holds today. I've clocked well over a thousand hours on mine to the point that my earcups were worn through (I replaced them with the awesome WC Freeze gel earpads ). SteelSeries released a successor - the Nova Pro Omni - earlier this year, but it currently sells for $380 and the improvements are certainly not worth the nearly $200 price premium. The Omni's pièce de résistance is its seamless cross-platform switching. If you predominantly use these headphones for one platform, then stick with the Nova Pros.

The one feature that undoubtedly makes the Nova Pro stand out amongst the crowd is the ingenious hot-swappable battery system . The Nova Pro includes two removable, rechargeable batteries: one to use in your headset and the other to remain charged and ready to go in a base station that doubles as a charger. This way, you get wireless freedom with zero downtime . Each battery lasts for up to 22 hours of continued use so you don't need to swap out too often.

The base station deserves additional mention. Not only does it charge your battery, it also features a clear and legible OLED display and a handy volume control knob. On the rear are USB inputs for connecting to your PC as well as an optional 3.5mm passthrough should you want to connect your speakers directly to the base station.

Of course a high end gaming headset is no good if it can't produce great sound and deliver vocal clarity. The Nova Pro is first and foremost a gaming headset, and it delivers big sound with its big 40mm neodymium dynamic drivers and 360° spatial sound effects (via SteelSeries Sonar for PC, Tempest 3D Audio for PS5, and Microsoft Spatial Sound for Xbox). The retractable boom mic is clear without any static and does a great job of canceling out ambient noise. My friends regularly point out that I sound like I'm in a quiet room because they hear nothing but my voice.

The Nova Pro is comfortable to use even during gaming marathons thanks to the suspension-style headband and comfortable leatherette ear cushions. You don't have to worry about babying it either, since the headband has a steel inner core. I've tossed mine around more times than I should have and it's still functionally perfect.

articles.headline: Shares in Musk's SpaceX plunge as tech and AI stocks fall
keyFacts: SpaceX and Tesla shares dropped significantly as tech and AI stocks plummeted following the Democratic victory in the US midterm elections.
Investors are concerned about potential tougher scrutiny of data center construction and fears that AI infrastructure investments may not deliver expected returns.
Tech leaders including OpenAI's Greg Brockman acknowledged the need to improve communication regarding the benefits of AI and data centers to local communities.
body: - Published
Shares in Elon Musk's SpaceX have plunged as tech and artificial intelligence stocks more broadly plummeted a day after the Democrats swept to victory in the midterms.
Those losses dragged the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite stock index down, which had fallen by more than 5% at one point in early trading.
The market has been reacting to possible tougher scrutiny of data centre construction and the artificial intelligence (AI) industry following Democrat wins in key data centre states including Texas.
Following the election, some tech leaders have acknowledged they need to improve their communication around data centres and the benefits of AI.
SpaceX shares were down more than 9% in by lunchtime in Thursday trading, while Tesla shares dropped more than 11%.

Musk had spent nearly $450m backing Republican campaigns, including at least $45m in support of Ken Paxton for the Texas senate seat, but Texas was turned blue in the Democratic tsunami on Tuesday night.
Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned heavily against data centres, pledging a moratorium on new construction in the sector.
Shares in chipmakers have been suffering, with AMD dropping more than 14% on Thursday, while Micron shares had dropped by as much as 17% before recovering slightly.
Intel shares are down by more than 7% and shares in Nvidia have fallen nearly 9%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had fallen by 10%.
The stock falls also hit the S&P 500 index, which dropped by 3.8% by lunchtime.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said the steep sell-off on the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 was sending shockwaves into other markets.
"Fresh panic over the AI trade has hit Wall Street hard," she said.

"Fears that the vast sums poured into AI infrastructure may not deliver the returns investors have been banking on are now colliding with the prospect of a sharp slowdown in data centre construction."
Some tech leaders have said they were caught off guard by the backlash against data centres in the midterms.
OpenAI president and co-founder Greg Brockman said he believed everyone had been surprised by the reaction to data centres, and more work needed to be done to ensure communities were on board.

"A lot of our shift over the course of this year has really been to realise that from San Francisco trying to build infrastructure in Texas, Georgia, and other places, you can't just tweet and say: 'This is going to be good.' You need to be in those communities," Brockman said at the WSJ Tech conference in Napa, California on Wednesday evening.
Meta's president Dina Powell McCormick agreed that the industry needed to improve their communication about the benefits of AI.
"I think we need to double and triple down on telling the story," she told the WSJ conference.
Alongside the immediate impacts of the US mid-term elections, some investors have become concerned that AI shares could be in a bubble that is due a correction.

articles.headline: Trump's European Far-Right Allies Suddenly Have A Problem With Him
keyFacts: European far-right politicians began distancing themselves from Donald Trump following the Democrats' victory in US midterm elections.
Several European leaders attributed the Republican defeat to the war with Iran and resulting cost of living pressures.
Analyst Mujtaba Rahman said European far-right leaders are distancing themselves to avoid Trump's growing unpopularity becoming an electoral liability.
body: LONDON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Europe’s far-right politicians have begun to distance themselves from Donald Trump following the Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections – but have mostly avoided directly criticising the president himself.

The realignment is notable as many of the leaders celebrated their ideological ties with Trump following his victory in 2024, with some of them visiting Washington DC since then and receiving backing from his billionaire ally Elon Musk.
Jordan Bardella, leader of France’s National Rally, which most polls suggest could form the next government, typified the political shift.

Trump’s second term was less isolationist than his first from 2017 to 2021, Bardella said. “American intervention regarding Iran carries very heavy consequences” for economies around the world, he added, without mentioning Trump as being behind that intervention.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, also attributed the loss to the Iran war. “Trump had promised his voters not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy ... This broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans,” she told news outlet T-Online.
Trump acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party’s losses but said he stood by his decision.
COST OF LIVING PRESSURES

In Italy, Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League party, which is part of the ruling coalition, said, “the American result was influenced above all by the wars, international tensions and the increase in the cost of living, the consequences of which fall directly on families.”
“The hope is that this vote can represent an acceleration towards the end of the conflicts and a return to peace,” he said.
Roberto Vannacci, a former Italian general who leads the far-right Futuro Nazionale party, said the US result showed the political dangers of failing to deliver on electoral promises.
Vannacci has previously expressed admiration for Trump’s “America First” brand of nationalist politics but has since criticised the president over foreign policy.

“Trump failed to live up to expectations, was unable to bring the war between Russia and Ukraine to an end and launched a war against Iran,” Vannacci told ANSA news agency, arguing that the resulting rise in energy prices and economic and stock market turmoil had hurt the US middle class and contributed to the election result.
TIES WITH TRUMP COULD BECOME AN ‘ELECTORAL LIABILITY’

Europe’s far-right leaders were distancing themselves from Trump for obvious political advantage, according to analyst Mujtaba Rahman, managing director of political risk consultancy Eurasia Group. “His growing unpopularity, particularly over the cost of living, risks turning what was once a political asset into an electoral liability,” he told Reuters.
Rahman said far-right leaders appeared to want it both ways: to reap the “ideological momentum of Trumpism” without being tarred by the “chaos and economic disruption of his presidency”.

“The risk is that Trump and his MAGA allies, who see Europe’s far right as ideological partners in their struggle against the European establishment, could respond by withdrawing their political support or even turning against them,” he added.

One of the few to play down the scale of the Republicans’ defeat was Dan Dungaciu, vice-president of the opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians, who argued that reports of Trump’s “political death” were “greatly exaggerated”.

He added, “Donald Trump does not automatically become a powerless president. Instead, he moves from a presidency backed by Republican majorities to one in which the executive and Congress will check each other much more intensely.”
In Spain, the leader of the far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal, made little attempt to temper his move away from Trump, telling reporters he was “in Spain and not in Michigan”.
“I care quite little about what happens in other places,” said Abascal, who has in the past touted his alliance with Trump and the MAGA movement.

Rupert Lowe, leader of the far-right Restore Britain party, also blamed the decision to attack Iran for the Republicans’ defeat, calling it a “catastrophic mistake.” He added, “What has this war achieved? Absolutely nothing of worth.” Lowe did not, however, include in his lengthy X post the name of the president who launched the war.

The right-wing populist Reform UK leader Nigel Farage acknowledged on Wednesday the election had been a “complete and utter rout” for Republicans, despite his earlier prediction that expectations of a Democratic landslide were overblown.

Farage, who has regularly touted his friendship with the US president and visited the White House last year, told GB News there was now “potential” for a rift between Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

“It turns out many of the young men, those who follow all sorts of right-wing influencers who voted for Trump in 2024, actually voted Democrat yesterday. It was a punishment beating, very much I think, because of the war, the extended war in Iran, and the cost of fuel,” Farage added.
